title: The Jew Vs. The World - Class Vayishlach
blurb: How Much Do We Compromise? How Much Do We Resist? We find contradicting perspectives on Jacob’s approach. Sometimes the Midrash and commentators seem to criticize Jacob for displaying subservience to Esau, going so far as to say that “Jacob awakened a sleeping robber,” and that it was his display of subservience that actually empowered Esau. After twenty years of working for Laban, Jacob begins his journey home, and now must confront the brother that he fled from so many years ago, Esau. Jacob chooses to initiate the meeting, and reaches out to Esau, sending messengers to ask for his favor and forgiveness. He also prepares an elaborate gift of herd after herd of sheep, goats, cows, donkeys, and camels. Then when Esau approaches Jacob shows him respect and humility, actually bowing down seven times. But other times we find that great Rabbis learned and emulated Jacob’s example in their own dealings with non-Jewish authorities. Indeed, in the time of the Second Temple, the Rabbis advocated surrender to the Romans and felt that it would have even prevented the destruction. How are we to reconcile this? And today, especially after the establishment of the State of Israel, the question is as relevant as ever: Do we compromise, or do we resist? Do we accommodate and adapt, or do we hold strong unflinchingly? Do we seek the favor of the world in which we live, or do we disregard its opinion? When do we surrender, and when do we rebel? title: Samach Vav Part 251: The only way to reach shuv is through total hanochas atzmuso to the Divine Will
blurb: Samach Vav p. 202-203: In addition, ratzo is easier than shuv because transcendence is the natural state of the revealed neshama (the outer dimension of its core etzem; not actually "outer," only relative to its core, similar to the level of ratzon -- the expression of the etzem, chitzoiniyus ub'hisgalus -- relative to taanug -- pnimiyus ub'heelem). Additionally, in a state of ratzo the soul feels more revealed G-dliness (though shuv generates a higher ohr atzmi, its complete revelation will only be in the future, while today it does not illuminate the soul as much as ratzo does). As such, it is increasingly very difficult to tear oneself away from ratzo, especially intense ratzo, and move into shuv. Thus, the only way to reach shuv is through total hanochas atzmuso, utter bittul to the Divine Will, seeded and rooted in Atzmus, which specifically desires shuv. Due to his intense bittul to the Divine Will, he puts himself in a state of shuv. This is kabolas ol Malchus Shomayim -- which is not driven by the person's feeling, pleasure and what is good for him. On his own, he would prefer to be in a state of klos ha'nefesh (his soul absorbed in its source), but due to his kabolas ol and total devotion, committed with his entire core to the Divine Will, that empowers him to be in a state of shuv.

title: Ep. 614: 14 Kislev: What Exemplifies a Loving Marriage and Shared Mission?
Mitteler Rebbe's Padah Beshalom part 5/9 שערי תשובה ד"ה פדה בשלום (פרק ו-ז)
blurb: Link to מאמר PDF⁠ Continuing to describe this level of "חיה" (the מקיף that becomes translated into פנימיות), the מיטעלער רבי explains that this is the רצון of the נפש האלקית. And while it indeed has the power of overwhelming the רצון of the נפש הבהמית, it does not transform the נפש הבהמית. The importance of this distinction is that even though the נפש האלקית is now in control, being that it did not transform the essence of the נפש הבהמית, the נפש הבהמית can always revert to its default and desire to go against Hashem, חס ושלום. The מיטעלער רבי gives a few examples of one element overpowering another one - whether quantitatively or qualitatively - where we see that even though it seems that the weaker element is transformed, we can understand that if the stronger element will subsequently be extracted, the weaker element will revert back to its original status.
